ann_31.text: This part acts on 80 of 242 training patients (33%), and only 9 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 45-year-old man with non-anginal chest pain, no ST depression and a maximum heart rate of 168 beats per minute), it slightly lowers the predicted risk, from about 4% to about 1% (on the training data only).

Through it, older age (42 to 66 years) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 12% to about 28%, and a higher maximum heart rate (118 to 175 beats per minute) lowers it from about 28% to about 22% (on the training data only).
Older age clearly raises the predicted risk only if the thallium scan shows no reversible defect (from about 12% to about 28%, while it stays at about 42% with a reversible defect).
Its rise with age is clearly larger if the maximum heart rate is above 152 beats per minute (from about 8% to about 27%, against about 18% to about 30% at or below 152).
A higher maximum heart rate clearly lowers the predicted risk more without a reversible thallium defect (from about 32% to about 20%, against about 46% to about 40% with one).

ann_32.text: This part acts on 117 of 242 training patients (48%), and 78 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with a flat ST segment, 1.4 mm of ST depression, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and a reversible thallium defect), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 87% to about 90% (on the training data only).
Through it, a flat ST segment, more ST depression and higher cholesterol each change the predicted risk only slightly (on the training data only).

Across the whole model, higher cholesterol clearly raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the ST segment is not flat (from about 18% to about 49%, against about 67% to about 88% with a flat ST segment).
The rise from more ST depression differs only slightly between patients with a flat ST segment (from about 75% to about 91%) and others (from about 28% to about 47%).

ann_33.text: This part acts on 121 of 242 training patients (50%), and 77 of them had heart disease.

For the typical patient it acts on (a 58-year-old man with 1.6 mm of ST depression, a flat ST segment, signs of left ventricular hypertrophy on the resting ECG and a reversible thallium defect), it slightly raises the predicted risk, from about 89% to about 91% (on the training data only).
Through it, more ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 47% (on the training data only).
ST depression adds risk here only once it rises above about 0.8 mm: going from 0 to 3.5 mm moves a typical patient from about 28% to about 56% (on the training data only).

ann_34.text: For a typical patient, the model clearly gives a lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 3%), non-anginal chest pain (about 5%) or atypical angina (about 14%) than with no chest pain symptoms (about 28%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 94%, a flat ST segment raises it to about 77%, higher cholesterol (193 to 308 mg/dL) from about 18% to about 49%, and higher resting blood pressure (110 to 155 mm Hg) from about 19% to about 43% (on the training data only).

More ST depression on exercise (0 to 2.8 mm) raises it from about 28% to about 47%, older age (42 to 66 years) from about 12% to about 28%, chest pain brought on by exercise to about 42%, and a reversible thallium defect to about 42% (on the training data only).

Being a woman lowers it from about 28% to about 3%, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 14%, and a maximum heart rate of 175 rather than 118 beats per minute from about 32% to about 20% (on the training data only).

The model has little data on three categories: a downsloping ST segment (17 patients; about 51%), an ST-T wave abnormality on the resting ECG (2 patients; about 46%) and a fixed defect on the thallium scan (15 patients; about 11%), all on the training data only.

ann_31.original: Heart-rate-reserve gate 1718 = ReLU(-0.812 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 0.762*thal:7 - 0.720*R3195), with relay R3195 = ReLU(0.981 + 1.073*thal:7). Hypothesis: 3195 is an always-on affine relay of thal:7 (thal:7 is one-hot, z-scored to {-0.769, 1.300}, so 3195 in {0.155, 2.376} > 0), which makes the gate's net thal:7 coefficient -1.535 and bias -1.518. The gate fires for patients whose achieved max heart rate is high for their age (thalach up, age down) AND who do NOT have a reversible thallium defect; its readout into the output is -0.582, so it is a protective (risk-lowering) term. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3195 is active for 100% of patients, so the gate reduces exactly to 1718 = ReLU(-1.518 - 1.490*age + 1.024*thalach - 1.535*thal:7). Active 33% overall: 51% of patients without a reversible defect vs 3% with one. Disease rate 11% when active vs 60% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: age 0.49 > thalach 0.34 > thal:7 (two copies) 0.25 each. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.938, the largest single nonlinear effect (readout logit SD 0.64). Supported.
ann_31.proposed: A part that acts on a third of patients, few of whom had heart disease; through it, older age raises the predicted risk only without a reversible thallium defect, and a higher maximum heart rate lowers it.

ann_32.original: Flat-ST-slope gate 1476 = ReLU(0.257 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.374*C3464), with C3464 = ReLU(1.300 + 1.011*chol). Hypothesis: a one-sided risk detector that opens for patients with a flat peak-exercise ST segment (slope:2), its height scaled by ST depression (oldpeak) and reduced by cholesterol via an almost-always-active affine chol relay (3464 is zero only when z-chol < -1.29). Readout into output +0.225 (raises risk). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 3464 is active for 93% (off only when z-chol < -1.29), so 1476 is nearly ReLU(-0.229 + 1.145*slope:2 + 0.770*oldpeak - 0.378*chol). Active for 98% of the 110 flat-slope patients vs 7% of the others, so it acts as a flat-slope indicator whose height rises with oldpeak (corr 0.69) and falls with cholesterol. Disease rate 67% when active vs 23% when inactive. Mean |sensitivity|: slope:2 0.55 > oldpeak 0.37 > chol 0.17. Removing its readout drops train AUC 0.943 -> 0.942 (logit SD 0.18). Supported. The negative chol term partly offsets chol's direct +0.613 edge for flat-slope patients; no clinical reading is offered for that.
ann_32.proposed: A part that acts on about half the patients and changes their predicted risk only slightly; through it, a flat ST segment, ST depression and cholesterol each have small effects.

ann_33.original: Oldpeak hinge pair: 1946 = ReLU(0.167 + 0.767*oldpeak) and 3284 = ReLU(-0.582 + 1.003*1946). Hypothesis: a convex piecewise-linear function of ST depression alone, with kinks at z-oldpeak = -0.218 (1946 opens) and 0.539 (3284 opens). Both exits read out positively (0.377 and 0.411), so beyond the second kink the logit slope in oldpeak roughly doubles: mild ST depression adds a little risk, marked ST depression adds much more. EVIDENCE (train, n=242): 1946 active 50% (disease rate 64%), 3284 active 24% (disease rate 79%). Contribution to the logit 0.377*1946 + 0.411*3284 has slope 0 below z-oldpeak -0.218, 0.289 between the kinks and 0.605 above 0.539. Mean |sensitivity| to oldpeak: 0.38 for 1946, 0.18 for 3284. Removing either readout changes train AUC by <= 0.001. Supported: a small convex ST-depression dose-response.
ann_33.proposed: ST depression on exercise above about 0.8 mm raises the predicted risk through this part.

ann_34.original: Root: logit z = -0.210 + LINEAR CORE - 0.582*age_hr_reserve_gate + 0.225*st_slope_chol_gate + 0.377*oldpeak_hinges[1946] + 0.411*oldpeak_hinges[3284]; prediction = sigmoid(z) (the genome output node is shown as ReLU, but for binary classification the evaluator applies a sigmoid, so z is a logistic score). LINEAR CORE (16 direct input->output edges, z-scored inputs): ca +1.68, cp:4 +0.99, sex:0 -0.74, chol +0.61, slope:2 +0.49, slope:1 -0.47, trestbps +0.47, sex:1 +0.45, cp:2 +0.42, fbs:1 -0.31, thal:7 +0.29, exang:1 +0.28, thal:6 -0.28, cp:1 -0.18, thalach -0.10, restecg:1 +0.07. The signs mostly match cardiology: more fluoroscopy-coloured vessels (ca), asymptomatic chest pain (cp:4), male sex, higher cholesterol and resting BP, flat ST slope and exertional angina raise risk, and upsloping ST (slope:1) lowers it. Exceptions are cp:2 +0.42 and fbs:1 -0.31, which run against the usual clinical direction and are left unexplained. Eight inputs are unused (cp:3, fbs:0, restecg:0, restecg:2, exang:0, slope:3, thal:3, thal:4). Age and oldpeak have no direct edge: they act only through the gates. COMPOSITION: purely additive in the logit. The three children add three nonlinear corrections to the linear core: (1) age_hr_reserve_gate, a protective ReLU that is on when max heart rate is high for the patient's age and there is no reversible thallium defect; (2) st_slope_chol_gate, a flat-ST-slope detector scaled up by oldpeak and down by cholesterol; (3) oldpeak_hinges, a convex two-kink dose-response in ST depression. The children share no hidden nodes. They are coupled only through shared input features (thal:7, thalach, chol and slope:2 also have direct edges, and oldpeak feeds both (2) and (3)). EVIDENCE (train, n=242): full model AUC 0.943, acc 0.884 (sigmoid(z) reproduces the evaluator exactly). Linear core alone gives AUC 0.930, so the nonlinear children add +0.013. Logit SD is 3.28 for the linear core vs 0.91 for all nonlinear readouts. Removing one readout at a time: 1718 -0.0057, 1476 -0.0017, 1946 -0.0007, 3284 -0.0004 AUC; all oldpeak-driven terms together -0.0064. Top SHAP features: ca, cp:4, sex:0, slope:2, slope:1 (all with direct edges). Interpretation: close to logistic regression, plus a protective heart-rate-reserve-for-age gate (blocked by a reversible defect) and two oldpeak/flat-slope ischaemia corrections.
ann_34.proposed: Typical angina, non-anginal chest pain and atypical angina lower the predicted risk compared with no chest pain symptoms. More vessels coloured, a flat ST segment, higher cholesterol, higher resting blood pressure, more ST depression, older age, chest pain on exercise and a reversible thallium defect raise it; being a woman, fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL and a higher maximum heart rate lower it.

summary.text: For a typical patient (a 56-year-old man with no chest pain symptoms and median test results, predicted risk about 28%), the model clearly gives a much lower predicted risk of heart disease with typical angina (about 3%), non-anginal chest pain (about 5%) or atypical angina (about 14%).

Going from 0 to 2 vessels coloured by fluoroscopy raises a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 94%, and a flat rather than upsloping ST segment at peak exercise raises it to about 77% (on the training data only).

Older age clearly raises the predicted risk, but only if the thallium scan shows no reversible defect: from 42 to 66 years it moves a typical patient from about 12% to about 28%, while with a reversible defect it stays at about 42%.

Higher cholesterol raises the predicted risk, and even more so if the ST segment is not flat at peak exercise: from 193 to 308 mg/dL it clearly moves from about 18% to about 49% without a flat ST segment, and from about 67% to about 88% with one.
Being a woman lowers a typical patient's predicted risk from about 28% to about 3%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL lowers it to about 14% (on the training data only).

confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_31.text: This part acts on 80 of 242 training patients (33%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 4% without this part to about 1% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 9 of these 80 patients had heart disease.

A higher age clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, but only if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan: for a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to about 28% if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan, and from about 42% to about 42% if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect.

A higher age clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if maximum heart rate is above 152 beats per minute: for a typical patient, age going from 42 years to 66 years moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 8% to about 27% if maximum heart rate is above 152 beats per minute, and from about 18% to about 30% if maximum heart rate is at or below 152 beats per minute.

A higher maximum heart rate clearly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan: for a typical patient, maximum heart rate going from 118 beats per minute to 175 beats per minute moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 32% to about 20% if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan, and from about 46% to about 40% if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect.

Through this part, maximum heart rate only slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 165 beats per minute for patients with a fixed defect on the thallium scan: for a typical such patient, going from 71 beats per minute to 182 beats per minute moves it from about 91% to about 87% (on the training data only).
